And finally, a plug for Green Business Partners. So keep that in mind as you're talking to businesses in your respective districts. With that, we'll jump into the first presentation, Solid Waste Management Plan update. I'll turn it over to Mr. Adams. Good afternoon, everyone, Chairman, members of the Board.

My name is Matthew Adams. I'm the division director in charge of the Engineering, Sustainability, and Environmental Compliance Group inside of the Solid Waste Management Program. With me today is Eric Forbes, the deputy director for the Solid Waste Management Program, as well as Chris Harrington, the director of DPWES.

And today, what I wanted to bring to your guys' attention or wanted to talk about is the 20-year Solid Waste Management Plan update, and its associated zero waste management plan that's due this year or due next year to DEQ by April of 2025. So a couple of key points that I wanted to talk about is today I wanted to talk about the board's community, the CCAP goals, and kind of what that means for the community and for the county. Two, I wanted to talk about, you know, the waste streams that are associated to that and how we plan to address those streams.

Three, I wanted to talk about the transformational strategies that we are currently considering when we're talking about how we move towards that goal for CCAP. And then finally, the third thing I wanted to talk about most importantly was some of the major infrastructure projects that are going to be necessary to meet that goal from a downstream end.

And finally, I was going to close with the timeline for those deliverables. So some of the important notes that come with this plan delivery, interactions with the community as well as when drafts and things like that are going to be due and how I'm going to interact with the board with those plans.

And then finally, we'll do questions. So first, the big thing I wanted to talk about is to do a quick recap. Currently, the CCAP goal for Fairfax County is 90% diversion of all waste from incineration by 2040.

So, you know, that's moving all of the waste streams that are currently inside of Fairfax County out of the landfill and out of the incinerator. Where we are currently, our current waste diversion rate, as defined by DEQ, is 43.9%.

So what does that mean? Currently, Fairfax County produces approximately 1.2 million tons of trash a year. Of that trash, of the waste that is generated, 630,000 tons of waste is processed as MSW that's sent to Covana every year.

That's approximately 252,000 Ford F-150s, to put it, to give it some perspective. That's what's moved through Fairfax County every single year as municipal solid waste. Now, we recently completed in April a waste composition study inside of our transfer station for Fairfax County waste.

Looking through that waste characterization study, we found that approximately 83% of the waste that is in our MSW or in the municipal solid waste that is sent out as trash every year is recoverable material. That is material that can be recovered, reduced, reused, finding a way to do source reduction to get rid of that waste.

So 83 percent. Now, doing the math, you know, backwards to try to get to that 90 percent goal based on our current diversion rate plus the diversion that could be done. We are forecasting that we would have to catch 100 percent of the trash and municipal 100 percent of the recyclables that go into the trash have to be captured to reach the C-cap goal.

So what that means is that approximately 500,000 tons of waste that is currently processed as MSW needs to find a new reuse or a new home as a recoverable material. The remaining 110,000 tons is, you know, things that aren't recoverable, things like diapers or things in the waste stream that we do not want, right, that have no secondary use.

So what does that mean for Fairfax County residents? Right now, the average resident inside of Fairfax County generates about a ton of waste a year on average. As the population increases inside of Fairfax County, so does the waste it creates.

And so does, as the county gets more economically stronger, the more waste it will create if we do not make substantial changes. We are looking at an estimated 1.4 million tons of waste by 2040 and 1.5 probably by 2060. This number continues to grow as the population grows. Now why that's important and what that means and what CCAP means to the county resident is that on average a county

resident produces five pounds of trash a day. That's two of these laptops. If we were to move to CCAP and move into that direction, a Fairfax County resident could throw one cell phone away. That's the total weight. That's half a pound is what they can get rid of every day. Now, when we move to 2040, if, you know, we don't make substantial changes or investments to our infrastructure, the amount of waste a resident throws away or that will be disposed of is two of these laptops and this phone put together. So the waste continues to increase. Now, currently,
Some of the strategies that we are looking at to kind of address this largest monumental task in front of us to reach 2040 and to reach 90% diversion is the zero waste strategies.

They're transformational strategies that we're starting to outline. Now, I want to be clear, we are currently in the process of analyzing each one of these strategies to look at cost, potential diversion impact, milestones to be completed, equity impacts.

We're looking at these at a lot of different lenses. We're trying to keep one Fairfax and the strategic plan in mind while we are looking through these strategies. So we do not have the data on their diversion rate as of right now, but as we continue along this process, I'll update the board accordingly. All right. So the first strategy that we were going to talk about is the education engagement evaluation enforcement. All of the strategies below education engagement evaluation enforcement will require educating the population on any

changes that we make. Educating the population in when residents move to Fairfax County, when we implement these new changes, they will produce waste in a different way. So they need to be instructed on how to do it, how we do it, how's the best way to mitigate that waste. So our outreach programs have to drastically improve to get into these communities and educate them on what we will be doing for waste and waste diversion and to meet our goals. Now with any good program, not only education, but there needs to be enforcement that goes along with that program. So as individuals

that as we change our code or implement some of these changes individuals that uh there needs to be an enforcement to go along with that so that we continue to make sure that the community and the rest of those waste streams are enforced properly right so one of the big things that we are talking about uh at a transformational strategy level is moving to a unified sanitation districts that is you know contracting hauling for all Fairfax County residents residents that's

a strategy that we're currently looking at and trying to weigh uh the benefits the pros and cons for that strategy and to see how much benefit it will provide to the county that's uh that's contracting out our municipal solid waste that recycling and yard waste as well as potentially some of our commercial activities. So two, the next thing is that one of the strategies that we're talking about is mandating recycling and composting for all Fairfax County residents.

That is single-family homes, multi-family, commercial properties. Everyone moves to a three-bin system of some kind, whether it is municipal solid waste, recycling, single-stream recycling and yard waste while you know commercial has a commercial multifamily may have a different three bin system we're looking at several options on how's the best way to implement that to get the largest amount of diversion for our community all right so then the next thing we were we continue to talk about is mandatory like implementing a mandatory pay-as-you-throw system there are a lot

of different options in which how to implement a pay-as-you-throw system whether it's by weight or by size of bin or size of bag that they purchased. There's several different ways to implement a pay-as-you-throw system, but we're currently evaluating which option works best for us inside of Fairfax County so that we can continue with the message and to promote source reduction inside of our community.

The more people that generate waste, there has to be an increased cost for them if we are to meet these goals. Next, we're going to talk a little bit about comprehensive commercial and multifamily programs. Currently inside of Fairfax County, commercial and multifamily programs are recycling and composting.

We have to expand those programs so that there is a requirement that every commercial business meets certain recycling goals inside of their business. I mean, commercial waste is about 60% of our waste stream.

It's one of the biggest pieces of the pie that's currently not being addressed as efficiently, as effectively as possible. So we have to create a comprehensive program around that. And finally, one of the things that we wanted to talk about was zero waste centers, is the implementation of zero waste centers within each of the communities to begin to have an outlet for some of these harder to recycle materials, an education center for residents that need to understand where waste gets deposited, where they can throw things away, where the reuse is.

It's a strategy at which to get the community involved with recycling and to make it a part of their everyday lives. So those are some of the big transformational strategies. Now, to implement those things, if we implement all of those, There is a substantial downstream end or downstream infrastructure investment that we are going to have to make.

Some of those large infrastructure projects that are going to be necessary are facilities called material recovery facilities, or MRFs is what they're referred to as. But material recovery facilities, we would need a minimum of at least three different types to address the separate waste streams that we're currently trying to address.

When waste is thrown away, the municipal solid waste, facilities will need to be constructed that go through and pick through the waste to target that 83% that we talked about previously. The 500,000 tons that have to be processed, municipal solid waste facilities are large-sized MRFs are the ones that are the type of facility that would need to be used to address those.

The same thing with our materials recovery facilities. We would need one for construction demolition debris. That's approximately 110,000 to 130,000 tons a year of CDD that's processed specifically just through our MSW that needs to be taken out of the waste stream and processed separately.

And finally, single stream recycling. The regional volume at which, well, the regional processing power for single stream, if we were to move all of our single stream or all of our potential recycling out and did source separation outside of the municipal solid waste stream, we do not have enough facilities to process that amount of material.

The private industry does not have it. We don't have one. There's nowhere in the region that we could take this material that could process it. So there would need to be substantial investment in that. Again, community zero waste centers, I talked about it briefly, but these are facilities that we would have to invest in locally inside of each either supervisor district or across the county where individuals could go and make it convenient for them to participate in some of our solid waste programs without having, you know, to make it easier for them as opposed to being able to just throw it away, right?

Another big infrastructure item that we have to talk about is a regional compost facility. Currently inside of, there are no compost facilities inside of Fairfax County. We're estimating that compost and food waste is roughly 250 to 300,000 tons of material a year.

It is a substantial amount of material, and currently there is nowhere outside of two very small facilities in our local jurisdiction or in our region that can handle that waste that's not inside of Maryland. There would have to be a substantial amount of investment in both food waste processing and in our regional compost facilities to be able to handle the significant amount of waste that we would generate.

All right, next. So now that we've kind of seen kind of some of our big strategies I've talked a little bit about and some of the big infrastructure I've talked about. Now, for the solid waste management plan, the timeline for delivery. On the slides, we are currently at the green dot.

The solid waste management program has already started focus group interactions with some of the communities that will be highly impacted by this plan. We've reached out to HVI communities, the hauling community, commercial property owners to start focus group interactions so that we can start hearing some of their concerns, what the problems that they're going to have, what they feel like they can participate in, so that we can start addressing those challenges as we go to implement the plan.

So that's our Tier 1 focus groups. That started this month. Tier 2 focus groups, we're going to start next month. That addresses, you know, some of our large players in schools. We're setting up focus groups in schools, non-vulnerable multifamily properties, as well as HOA.

We're trying to get HOA representation so that we can hear from those communities as well to see what the impacts of this plan and what some of these large transformational strategies may have on them. The next thing is what I would believe is one of the most important things that we will do.

We will start a public input campaign, a large open input campaign for all Fairfax County residents. We are scheduling that to start in July and run for 30 days. So it will start in July and end in August. And it will be an open public input survey out to everyone.

And it will be a large outreach campaign so that everyone in the county will be able to participate. We are really pushing for input from the community so we can hear from them, see what they like, see what they don't like, see what's meaningful and what's beneficial to them, and how is the best way to implement some of our plans.

Also on the timeline, there's consistent meetings. The board's environmental committee, we have listed those on the timeline. And as we get data or as we move through this plan, I'd like to bring consistent updates to the Environmental Board Committee so that we keep informed and stay on track for the inevitable public hearing that we're aiming to be in February of 2025.

Finally, the last piece is the plan delivery timeline. So the first draft of our plan for the transformational strategies, our infrastructure investment, all of those initial plans will be drafted, ready to go, should be in July of 2024.

A second draft will be in September. A final draft should arrive at the end of November with a submission to the board in December and a potential vote in March. And finally, ending in a April 16th, 2025, delivery to DEQ upon approval of the board.

Thank you, and good afternoon, Mr. Chairman and members of the Board of Supervisors. I'm John Morrill, Director of the Office of Environmental and Energy Coordination. I'm joined by John Silcox, our public information officer, who will co-present this discussion.

We are presenting for your consideration a new emphasis on residential programming as we pursue clean energy to reduce emissions that cause climate change. For context, the three broad strategies that are essential to achieving the goal of carbon neutrality in Fairfax County are increased use of renewable energy, such as solar power, widespread use of electric vehicles by individuals, businesses, and in public transit, and increased energy efficiency in existing buildings, especially homes.

Fairfax already promotes regional group purchasing programs, such as the Solarize effort that has led to over 400 rooftop solar installations in the county since 2015. This program is managed by the Virginia nonprofit Local Energy Alliance Program, or LEAP.

We are now promoting a second group purchasing program, Solar Switch, which is increasing awareness of the solar opportunities to residents throughout the region. This program is run by the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors organization and operates in the capital region.
These nonprofits running these programs can provide technical assistance to prospective customers, and that has been a positive that informs our recommendation today.

The county is electrifying its fleet of transit vehicles, and we offer information, its overall fleet, that is, and we offer information and incentives to homeowner associations to assist in the installation of electric vehicle charging infrastructure.

Generous federal incentives are available not only for new vehicles, but also for used electric vehicles. In the case of used EVs, the incentives are subject to income qualification to encourage more widespread use of EVs among less advantaged drivers.

We make available a lot of information on our website, but continue to field many inquiries about EVs and charging. And last, OEEC provides information and resources about incentives and information to residents on home energy efficiency, partnering with several other agencies and community groups to reach households with guidance to lower energy costs and improve home comfort.
